If the certification issue remains unresolved, Nepal risks losing platforms worth a combined $19.7 million (approximately Rs3 billion). Another Mi-17 also reportedly remains grounded at Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu, awaiting component overhauls and repairs.

The external shocks surrounding the Mi-17s are not unique to a single aircraft or country of origin. The Bell helicopters being acquired under FMF benefit from having a large, global commercial support network that may reduce some of the supply chain vulnerabilities associated with the Mi-17s. Nevertheless, Nepal will continue to rely on an international maintenance ecosystem, inherently susceptible to external disruptions, throughout the aircraft lifecycle.

A greater fleet commonality with the Bell variants will improve institutional sustainment capacity by reducing the complexity of maintaining multiple, parallel foreign-origin aircraft. However, as the Bell fleet assumes a larger share of Nepal’s disaster-response capability, long-term aircraft availability could become concentrated within a single OEM support ecosystem. Consequently, Nepal’s expanding inventory of foreign aircraft necessitates strengthening the domestic maintenance ecosystem alongside international support agreements to reduce future vulnerability.

As Nepal expands the Bell helicopter fleet across both military and civilian operators, the growing commonality in airframes presents an opportunity to establish a more coordinated national approach to organisational-level maintenance where operational security permits.

Nepal should gradually build shared technical capacity through common training pipelines, standardised maintenance procedures, specialised tooling and spare parts management. A coordinated domestic maintenance ecosystem would improve resource utilisation and reduce duplication of technical investments, maximising the institutional efficiencies of fleet commonality. Over time, Nepal could reduce long-term reliance on a single OEM support ecosystem for routine maintenance activities while maintaining international support agreements for OEM-certified depot-level maintenance and military-specific requirements.

Nepal’s domestic maintenance capacity must be supported by stronger evidence-based lifecycle planning that simultaneously advances both self-reliance and long-term international maintenance partnerships. Nepal should institutionalise a centralised digital asset management system to monitor aircraft utilisation rates, maintenance cycles, component reliability, and spare parts consumption without disclosing operationally sensitive information. The system can provide a common evidence base to identify recurring maintenance bottlenecks and turnaround timelines, while informing decisions on which capabilities to develop domestically and which to retain through international partnerships. A comprehensive fleet performance database will improve forecasting of lifecycle costs, strengthening Nepal’s overall negotiating position in future acquisition and maintenance arrangements.

articles.title: RSP must turn its parliamentary initiative into results
articles.summary:
Last week, a meeting of the House of Representatives scheduled to discuss a bill was adjourned due to the absence of the minimum number of lawmakers required to conduct the meeting. Nepal’s statute requires at least one-fourth of the total strength, or 69 lawmakers, to be present for a House meeting to commence. However, only 61 lawmakers were present, prompting the Speaker to adjourn the meeting. While it is the responsibility of every lawmaker to ensure regular attendance, the onus of ensuring that the House functions smoothly lies with the ruling party. The Rastriya Swatantra Party commands 182 seats, which is two and a half times the minimum number required for the House to get down to business.

It was complete negligence on the part of a party with close to a two-thirds majority to leave Parliament without the minimum presence of lawmakers just four months after the House began its work. Even though this was the first such incident involving the full House, meetings of House committees have previously been postponed for the same reason.

However, in a timely intervention, the party is taking serious measures to ensure that its lawmakers do not merely mark their attendance and skip House proceedings. It has asked every lawmaker to fill out a Google Form providing details of their attendance and to notify the party in advance if they cannot attend a meeting. The party leadership believes the move will make parliamentary meetings more organised and effective, and rightly so.

The RSP rose to power by capitalising on the ineffective performance of the legacy parties on multiple fronts, including Parliament. The two previous HoRs elected after the promulgation of the Constitution of Nepal were not productive. The internal feud within the then Nepal Communist Party disrupted the functioning of the House elected in 2017. Then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli dissolved the House twice, effectively cutting its working period by about a year. The House elected in 2022 also became mired in repeated obstruction. The Nepali Congress blocked proceedings for weeks, demanding a probe into RSP chair Rabi Lamichhane’s alleged involvement in cooperative fraud. The RSP later obstructed the House, seeking an investigation into the visit visa scam, while the CPN-UML did the same over alleged gold smuggling.

That House eventually met an early demise following its dissolution after the Gen Z protests in September. Most of the tenure of previous two Houses was spent in the making and unmaking of governments, with less focus on its core job of enacting laws and holding fruitful discussions.

As a result, the previous Houses could not even promulgate the laws necessary for the full-fledged implementation of the Constitution. History should not repeat itself. The third House since the promulgation of the Constitution needs to correct the shortcomings of its predecessors. The initiative the RSP is taking to keep track of its lawmakers’ attendance is a positive step towards that effort.

The Balendra Shah government has set a target of promulgating 166 laws through Parliament in the current fiscal year. Making that happen requires effective functioning of Parliament and its mini-Houses—the parliamentary committees. That, in turn, requires the active participation of lawmakers and proper facilitation by the government. The RSP leadership seems to have understood this fact. Now, it needs to translate that understanding into implementation.

articles.title: Ex-Gorkhas seek recruitment revival as Indian Army chief visits Nepal
articles.summary:
Former Gorkha soldiers who served in the Indian Army have urged visiting Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth to resume recruitment of Nepali youths, which has remained suspended since 2020.

Gaj Bahadur Thapa, central vice-president and Gandaki Province coordinator of the Nepal Bharatiya Gorkha Sainik Board, raised the issue with General Seth after an event at the Pension Paying Office in Ram Bazaar, Pokhara. The Indian Army chief had been in Pokhara before he wrapped up his four-day visit to Nepal on Wednesday.

“We have been raising our voice for Gorkha recruitment, and you must also address it,” Thapa told Seth, drawing applause from fellow veterans gathered at the facility.

Seth did not make a concrete commitment to resuming recruitment under India’s Agnipath scheme. The issue was also left out of the high-level formal discussions held in Kathmandu before he returned to India on Wednesday.

The Agnipath scheme did not feature in Seth’s meeting with Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who also holds the defence portfolio, or in delegation-level talks with Chief of Army Staff General Ashok Raj Sigdel.

Nepali Army spokesman Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet said the formal discussions focused mainly on bilateral military relations, joint training and strategic cooperation. The primary purpose of Seth’s visit was the conferral of the honorary rank of General of the Nepali Army, a senior army official said.

Nepalis’ recruitment into the Indian Army was suspended in 2020 following the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic and remained frozen through 2021. India introduced the Agnipath scheme on June 14, 2022, replacing traditional recruitment with a short-service model under which personnel aged 17 to 23, known as Agniveers, serve four-year terms.

Under the scheme, recruits receive a lump-sum payment of around 1.2 million Indian rupees at the end of their service, but do not receive lifelong pensions or medical coverage.

The scheme triggered widespread protests in India and strong reservations in Nepal. Concerns in Kathmandu centred on the potential social and national security implications of returning short-service military personnel without pension security.

The government led by then-prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba subsequently halted Gorkha recruitment pending a formal bilateral understanding, maintaining that unilateral changes to the recruitment system should not be applied to Nepali recruits without prior consultation.

According to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the agenda for Seth’s visit was prepared by the Bilateral Group on Security Issues, comprising officials from the defence and foreign ministries of both countries and senior military officers.

The Agnipath scheme was not included in the group’s framework, officials said. Nepali foreign ministry officials had prepared responses in case their Indian counterparts raised the issue, but no such discussion took place during the visit.

Seth’s visit came amid growing pressure from former Gorkha soldiers, their families and prospective recruits. A week before his arrival, ex-Gorkha associations submitted memorandums to the Nepali government through local administration offices in six major cities.

In Pokhara, the Indian Ex-Gorkha Brigade organised a rally involving veterans, their families and prospective recruits. Participants marched from Pokhara Stadium to the District Administration Office at Sahid Chowk, calling on the government to intervene diplomatically to resume recruitment.

Recruitment and pension concerns

Nepalis’ service in the Indian military dates back more than two centuries, to 1815, following the Anglo-Nepal War and the subsequent peace treaty with the British East India Company.

Over the decades, Gorkha troops have become an important part of Nepal-India military ties, while their pensions and post-retirement benefits have also contributed to the economies of communities across Nepal.

An estimated 36,000 Nepali citizens currently serve in the Indian Army, while around 125,000 Indian Army veterans live in Nepal. The Pension Paying Office in Pokhara alone serves about 60,000 ex-servicemen and their dependants.

Before recruitment was suspended in 2020, around 1,400 Nepali youths were recruited into the Indian Army each year from more than 5,000 applicants who competed in physical and academic examinations held in major urban centres.

Veterans also used Seth’s visit to raise concerns about delays in family pension payments.

Thapa said Nepali youths recruited before 1990 were often enlisted primarily based on physical fitness, without stringent documentation requirements such as citizenship certificates, birth certificates and marriage registrations. Family pensions for widows were introduced only after 1984, during the tenure of Indian prime minister Indira Gandhi, he said.

The lack of documentation from that period has since created discrepancies between Nepali citizenship records and Indian military records over names, spellings and dates of birth.

Thapa estimated that 8,000 to 10,000 widows of former Gorkha soldiers in Nepal are currently unable to claim their pensions because of such discrepancies.

“A name or age on a local citizenship card often differs slightly from military service books,” Thapa said. “Neither the government of Nepal nor the government of India has taken proactive steps to simplify verification.”

He urged Seth to allow pension claims to be verified through photographs and biometric thumbprints instead of requiring exact documentary matches. He also called on the Nepali government to simplify its administrative verification procedures.

Seth assured the veterans that the Indian Army would make every effort to address the welfare concerns of former Gorkha soldiers.

He left Nepal on Wednesday after completing his four-day visit and was seen off at the Tribhuvan International Airport by Lieutenant General Pradeep Jung KC and his wife.

articles.title: Indian Army chief Seth returns home after four-day Nepal visit
articles.summary:
Indian Army chief General Dhiraj Seth and his wife, Komal Seth, returned home on Tuesday after completing a four-day official visit to Nepal at the invitation of Nepali Army chief General Ashok Raj Sigdel.

They were seen off at Tribhuvan International Airport by Lieutenant General Pradip Jung KC and his wife.

During the visit, President Ramchandra Paudel conferred on Seth the honorary rank of general of the Nepali Army. Seth also held separate courtesy meetings with President Paudel, Prime Minister Balendra Shah and General Sigdel.

Seth arrived in Kathmandu on Sunday for the visit at Sigdel’s invitation. Prime Minister Shah, who also holds the defence portfolio, received Seth at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers on Monday. Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava also attended the meeting.

The visit came as Nepal and India continued a longstanding military tradition under which the army chiefs of the two countries are awarded the honorary rank of general in each other’s armies.

The practice dates back to 1950 and is regarded as a symbol of the close cultural, religious, historical and military ties between the two countries. Under the tradition, the Nepali Army chief receives the honorary rank of general of the Indian Army, while the Indian Army chief is conferred the honorary rank of general of the Nepali Army.

articles.title: High Court orders police not to arrest journalist Kishor Shrestha
articles.summary:
The Patan High Court on Wednesday issued an interim order directing police not to arrest or detain Kishor Shrestha, chairman and editor of Jana Aastha Prakashan, over a news article published in his weekly newspaper.

A single bench of judge Achyut Kuikel ordered the District Police Range, Lalitpur, not to arrest, detain, or exert pressure on Shrestha until a final decision is reached on the prohibition petition filed by the editor.

The order follows a complaint lodged with the Press Council Nepal over a news report titled “Improve yourself Madam, there is still time”, published in Jana Aastha on August 12. Fearing possible arrest while the Press Council was reviewing the complaint, Shrestha had moved the High Court seeking a writ of prohibition.

In its ruling, the High Court noted that the matter was already under consideration by the Press Council and remained unresolved.

The court highlighted that constitutional guarantees of freedom of opinion and expression, the right to communication, and precedent set by prior Supreme Court rulings justified the issuance of the interim order.

The High Court has given the District Police Range, Lalitpur, 15 days to submit a written response regarding Shrestha’s petition.

articles.title: Shahi wins confidence vote to lead Karnali government
articles.summary:
Karnali Province Chief Minister Mangal Bahadur Shahi has secured a vote of confidence from the provincial assembly, three weeks after taking office.

Shahi received 21 votes in Wednesday’s provincial assembly meeting, the minimum required to command a majority in the 40-member House. Thirty-six lawmakers were present. Thirteen voted against the motion, while two remained neutral.

Shahi was appointed chief minister on July 28 with the support of the CPN-UML after Yamalal Kandel resigned from the post. Shahi, the parliamentary party leader of the Nepali Communist Party, has the backing of 14 NCP lawmakers and 10 from the UML, including the Speaker.

The provincial assembly has 15 Nepali Congress lawmakers, one independent former chief minister, Raj Kumar Sharma, and one Rastriya Prajatantra Party lawmaker.

Speaker Nanda Gurung announced that Shahi had secured the confidence of the House after a majority voted in favour of his motion.

Before the vote, Shahi urged all parties, including the Congress, to support his government, saying Karnali’s poverty, illiteracy and geographical remoteness should be treated as the province’s main challenges rather than the arithmetic of power.

Shahi had remained the only member of his cabinet since his appointment, as the NCP and UML struggled to agree on the distribution of ministries.

The two coalition partners reached a six-point agreement on Wednesday afternoon, clearing the way for the expansion of the provincial cabinet.

Shahi’s appointment followed Kandel’s resignation after serving as chief minister for around two years.

articles.title: Bara residents block highway over rape, murder of four-year-old girl
articles.summary:
Residents blocked the highway in Simara on Wednesday afternoon to protest the rape and murder of a four-year-old girl who had been missing for three days from Bhaktinagar in Jitpur Simara-1.

The protesters began blocking the Birgunj-Pathlaiya section of the Tribhuvan Highway at around 1pm, demanding the arrest and severe punishment of those responsible and relief for the victim’s family.

The girl, Garima Chaudhary, had gone missing from her home on Sunday. Her body was found on Tuesday evening. Police said she had been lured from her home with a chocolate and taken to an abandoned house nearby, where she was raped and killed.

The body remains at the Kalaiya Provincial Hospital. Her relatives had not initially come to claim it as they had yet to file a police complaint.

Garima was a student in the early childhood development class at the local Saraswati Primary School.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Min Bahadur Ghale, spokesperson for the Bara District Police Office, said police had confirmed that the girl was raped and murdered. He said those allegedly involved had been identified and arrested and that further investigation was underway.

Police have arrested Suman Thapa, 17, a helper on a local passenger minivan, and Progres Chaudhary, 24, the vehicle owner from Simara-1, among others in connection with the case, Ghale said.

He said a complaint had since been filed on behalf of the victim’s family and the process of handing over the body had begun.

The hospital administration, however, said the body was still at the hospital because it had not received the required letter and police complaint from the authorities to release it.

articles.title: Landslide survivors and rescuers fall ill in Rolpa
articles.summary:
Residents displaced by a deadly landslide in Rolpa and those involved in the rescue effort are beginning to face health problems after days of exposure to rain, poor living conditions and inadequate food and rest. Many displaced families are still sleeping away from their homes, while some rescuers have fallen ill after spending days searching for bodies and survivors.

Health workers in Thabang Rural Municipality-5 say people forced to live in temporary shelters are reporting various health problems. Those involved in the rescue operation have also become physically weak after working continuously in wet conditions following the landslide that killed 13 people in Kotalbara last week.

Duk Pun Magar, 54, is among those who have fallen ill. A resident of Nanbang in Uwa, Pun Magar spent two to three days after the landslide helping search for the dead, injured and missing, recover bodies and arrange safe shelter for survivors.

He is now receiving treatment for typhoid at the health post in Kotalbara. He had a fever from the start of the rescue operation but kept working because the search-and-rescue effort was the priority.

“I was in Kotalbara on that terrifying evening of August 12. I saw and experienced the landslide from close range,” Pun Magar said. “I managed to escape with my life, but I could not save many others.”

He said the heavy rain and sudden roar of the landslide gave people little time to react.

“On one side there was heavy rain, and on the other came the landslide with a huge, terrifying roar. We barely had time to save ourselves,” he said.

Pun Magar and other rescuers continued working in the rain after the landslide, searching beneath collapsed houses for bodies and helping survivors move to safer places. Many spent long hours soaked through and often went without regular meals.

“We even had to eat junk food to keep our hunger at bay,” Pun Magar said. “Because we could not eat on time, our bodies became weaker, and I eventually fell ill.”

He has been receiving treatment since Monday. Health worker Nim Subedi said his condition had improved after treatment began. Many other people involved in the rescue operation have also fallen ill, Subedi said.

Bimarsa Gharti Magar, another health worker at the health post, said displaced people were also being brought in for treatment after developing health problems while staying outside their homes.

“We have urged everyone to remain alert given the situation after the landslide,” Bimarsa said. “We have also advised residents of Upper Uwa and nearby villages who have been forced to stay outside their homes to take their health seriously.”

The health concerns come as residents continue to live under the threat of further landslides. The disaster in Kotalbara has left surrounding communities deeply traumatised, and many residents say they become frightened as soon as rain begins.

Around five or six families living near Kotalbara leave their homes after dark and take shelter at the local health post. They return home during the day to work in their fields and eat their meals.

“We have asked those who find it difficult to stay in their homes to take shelter at the health post,” Subedi and Bimarsa said. “They can eat, spend the night there and avoid the risk of another landslide.”

Several families in Uwa Thulogau are also spending their nights at nearby schools, while others have moved temporarily to relatives’ homes.

“People are still frightened. Those who feel at risk spend the night at schools, while some consider relatives’ homes safer and stay there,” said Dhukaman Roka Magar, a local community leader and social worker. “For now, there are no other alternatives available.”

Some families continue to stay in their homes, while others have been advised to spend the night in their cattle sheds. Those taking shelter elsewhere return home during the day to carry on with their daily work.

The continuing rain has made the situation more difficult. Residents say the loss of homes and relatives in the neighbouring settlement remains fresh in their minds, while the possibility of another landslide keeps them from sleeping comfortably in their homes.

Six or seven families, including those of Jaman Roka Magar, Ajambar Pun Magar, Lata BK, Fista BK, Naumala BK and Bujhimala BK of Uwa Thulogau, have been spending every night elsewhere in search of safer shelter.

Moving away from homes where they have lived for years has created additional difficulties. Families in the Kotalbara area, including those of Man Kumari Pun Magar, Farki Gharti Magar, Karmajit Pun Magar, Mek Roka Magar and Junosh Roka Magar, have also been forced to seek alternative shelter.

“We stay at home during the day, but we do not dare sleep there at night or when it starts raining,” said resident Sanju Pun Magar. “When I remember the sound of the landslide and what happened that night, I am afraid it could happen again.”

Residents are using schools, the health post, relatives’ homes and cattle sheds as temporary shelters. With no permanent safe accommodation available, their daily lives have become a cycle of spending the day at home and the night in temporary shelters.

Following the heavy loss of life in Kotalbara, residents have urged the government to reassess the risks facing the settlement and arrange temporary as well as long-term relocation to safer areas.

The landslide killed 13 people and damaged at least six houses, cattle sheds, shops and other structures, according to Rolpa Chief District Officer Ganga Bahadur Chhetri.

Three or four of those killed had no immediate family members, Chhetri said, complicating efforts to provide relief.

“In such cases, rather than simply providing relief, we first need to identify their relatives. If there are none, we have to find another option,” he said. “But we need the final findings of the investigation before making a decision.”

Chhetri also said it was unfortunate that relief supplies had not reached Kotalbara in the quantities expected and that the single-door system announced by the local administration had not been fully implemented.

He said the authorities needed to relocate displaced families to safer areas, with local, provincial and federal governments working together on the plan. The local units, he added, would have to play a central role in managing the landslide victims and their relocation.

articles.title: Home minister tells RSP lawmakers to keep party disputes out of Parliament
articles.summary:
Home Minister Sudan Gurung has urged lawmakers from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) not to bring internal party grievances into Parliament, saying that doing so would strengthen the opposition.

At the RSP parliamentary party meeting on Wednesday, Gurung also asked the party’s lawmakers not to criticise the government in Parliament.

According to an RSP lawmaker who attended the meeting, Gurung urged MPs to support the government’s work.

“Let’s keep our internal disputes within the party and not oppose the government in Parliament. The opposition is starting to grow stronger,” Gurung told the lawmakers, according to the participant.

Gurung also asked lawmakers to direct any complaints concerning the Home Ministry to his personal secretary rather than raising them directly with him.

“If you have any complaints related to the Home Ministry, don’t bring them to me. Speak to my personal secretary James Karki and meet with him,” Gurung told the lawmakers. He also gave them his personal secretary Karki’s new phone number.

RSP chair Rabi Lamichhane had called the parliamentary party meeting for 11am on Wednesday. Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who is also the RSP parliamentary party leader, did not attend the meeting.

Lamichhane is leading the meeting in his absence. Most government ministers are attending.

articles.title: Congress pulls plug on Koshi government
articles.summary:
The Nepali Congress has withdrawn its support for the Koshi provincial government, putting further pressure on Chief Minister Hikmat Kumar Karki as he faces the prospect of having to seek a fresh vote of confidence.

A meeting of the Nepali Congress parliamentary party in Koshi on Wednesday decided to withdraw support for the government led by Karki.

The party sent a formal letter to the Koshi Provincial Assembly Secretariat while the parliamentary party meeting was still underway, provincial assembly secretary Sudarshan Khadka said. The Congress has also informed the assembly that its lawmakers will now sit on the opposition benches.

The Congress has 29 lawmakers in the 93-member provincial assembly. Its withdrawal from the government leaves Karki facing a tougher political test and could trigger another round of negotiations among the parties over the formation of a new governing coalition.

Karki had urged the Congress to support his government in a vote of confidence. Instead, the Congress parliamentary party decided to withdraw the support it had already extended to the government, effectively ending its participation in the ruling coalition.

The Congress had joined the provincial government under a power-sharing arrangement with the CPN-UML. Its decision to pull out comes as the coalition between the two parties has come under strain.

Karki will now be required to seek a vote of confidence in the provincial assembly. With no party holding a majority on its own in the 93-member assembly, the withdrawal of the Congress is likely to reopen negotiations over the next governing arrangement.

Parties will have to reassess their numbers and explore possible alliances as Karki seeks to keep his government in office. The immediate focus will be on whether he can secure enough support from other parties to survive the confidence vote.

articles.title: Government pushes ministries to meet FATF reform targets
articles.summary:
The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers has directed government secretaries to work on a fixed timeline and take effective measures to get Nepal off the Financial Action Task Force’s “grey list”, a global watchlist for countries with weaknesses in their efforts to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.

A meeting of government secretaries chaired by chief secretary Govinda Bahadur Karki on Tuesday reviewed the government’s efforts to secure Nepal’s removal from the grey list. Nepal has prepared an action plan to address the deficiencies identified by the FATF, and the meeting decided that all ministries and government agencies must implement the plan effectively and within the prescribed deadlines.

The Prime Minister’s Office will regularly monitor implementation and assess whether ministries and agencies are meeting the commitments set out in the action plan. Relevant ministries and agencies will also be required to provide the office’s monitoring team with regular updates on their progress.

Nepal was placed on the FATF grey list on February 21, 2025, and has been given a set of measures to complete before it can be removed. The government has two years to address the shortcomings identified by the FATF. Failure to make sufficient progress could increase the risk of Nepal being placed on the FATF’s blacklist, which would make international financial transactions more difficult and raise the country’s financial and reputational risks.

The government has set a target of completing the required reforms by mid-February 2027.

An Asia-Pacific Group delegation of the FATF visited Nepal in May and raised concerns during meetings with government officials about areas where the country had made insufficient progress. The delegation also expressed concern over the slow implementation of Nepal’s action plan.

The areas identified as needing further work include regulation of banks and financial institutions, oversight of cooperatives, banking offences, real estate transactions and precious-metal trading. The delegation also flagged shortcomings in the regulation, investigation and prosecution of corruption, tax evasion, human trafficking and smuggling, environmental and wildlife crimes, and money laundering through shell companies.

The secretary-level meeting also decided to prioritise reforms that require immediate action and can produce tangible improvements for citizens. Ministries and agencies have been instructed to submit regular progress reports to the Prime Minister’s Office.

The meeting also decided to observe Civil Service Day on September 7 at the federal, provincial and local levels. The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration has been tasked with preparing the programme framework.

The secretaries also agreed to review the implementation of governance reform procedures, guidelines, directives and circulars issued by the Prime Minister’s Office, as well as progress made under them.

The meeting further decided that ministries and agencies should resolve policy and administrative problems affecting their work through coordination among the relevant secretaries. Issues that cannot be resolved at that level should be referred to the Prime Minister’s Office for coordination and a decision.

The government has also designated fiscal year 2026-27 as the “Year of Lawmaking and Reform”. The meeting called for existing laws to be updated or repealed where necessary and for new legislation to be drafted to reflect current needs.

It also directed ministries and agencies to immediately begin public procurement procedures for programmes and projects covered by the government’s “zero-day procurement policy” where procurement processes have not yet started.

The decisions come as the government faces pressure to demonstrate concrete progress on the reforms required for Nepal to exit the FATF grey list within the agreed timeframe.

articles.title: Movie review: In ‘Chiso Maanchhe’, a journey with a corpse becomes a meditation on grief and human connection
articles.summary:
There are not many Nepali filmmakers willing to trust their audience to understand their film without announcing its intentions through dialogues. Dipendra K Khanal, however, seems to have given us a space to sit with his images, silences and ambiguities to make sense of ‘Chiso Maanchhe’ on our own.

Released in the theatres in 2022 and on YouTube in 2025, the film begins with a rolling wheel as the radio announces the number of deaths in Nepal during the coronavirus pandemic. Ashok (played by Arpan Thapa) has a mask hanging under his chin and a sanitiser on the edge of his truck’s window.

Ashok, a driver, is hired to take a corpse from Kathmandu to Bajura in his truck. This is a corpse that has freshly arrived from Qatar, one of the major destinations for Nepali migrant workers. Accompanying Ashok are a grieving father, Sher Bahadur (Deshbhakta Khanal), and a widowed wife (Swastima Khadka). The wheels roll and the journey begins.

As they travel from Kathmandu to Bajura, they encounter the broader terror of the widespread virus with the roads engulfed by corpses, migrants, police, and youth patrols. Some go along with them and others obstruct their passage.

With them moving, stopping, negotiating, rebelling and starting again, the story becomes an emblem of the precariousness of life. Along with this, the characters, initially entirely as strangers, begin to understand each other’s worlds, and more importantly, their own.

Khanal, also the director of ‘Aama’, ‘Pashupati Prasad’, ‘Ke Ghar Ke Dera’, is best known for depicting social issues and everyday struggles in his films and he continues doing so in ‘Chiso Maanchhe’. The film shows a broader picture of a frozen, individualistic and isolated society.

In a scene, Khadka’s character is found frolicking in the woods, as though she stumbled upon an oasis. Her father-in-law calls her out, quickly and furiously, and says, “If this was the old days, you would’ve had to become a sati.” The sati is a historical custom where a widow self-immolates on her deceased husband’s funeral pyre.

“If not physically, I have been made a sati in heart,” she says.

It is a line the film never explains, and doesn't need to, because by then, Khanal has already taught us to read what isn't said. Non-verbal cues in the film stand monumental for its provocative ways to communicate its themes and the characters’ emotions.

The truck carrying the corpse of Damber Bahadur, who died of “heart failure” in Qatar, has a quote painted on its back in red. “Life goes on with happiness and laughter. If we work hard, we can find gold in our own country.”

The irony is stark and unmistakable.

Further, these non-verbal cues particularly elaborate the dynamics between Ashok, the driver, and the daughter-in-law.

Whether it’s buying her a bag of titaura to satisfy her cravings or extinguishing his cigarette when she looks uncomfortable, these small, wordless gestures create a sense of intimacy throughout their journey.

With this screenwriting, as commendable as to earn him the ‘Best Writer Award’ for the film, Khanal, however, fails to depict the nuances of his female character. He neither gives a promising background to the daughter-in-law nor a name.

Khadka’s character attempts to run away before retrieving her husband’s dead body. Later, she is found staring at a poster that showed the winner of ‘Nepal Idol’, a singing reality show. We understand consequently that her dream was to become a singer, and that the marriage had not given her enough reasons to grieve her dead husband.

She is given a dream. And a somewhat rebellious nature to chase it. But not enough to earn her a platform of her own.

However, Khadka’s body language, dialect, eye contacts, and even the way she blinks are carefully curated habits to build her character which results in a memorable depiction despite being written unidimensionally.

Ashok, on the other hand, gets to reminisce about his dead wife and six-month-old child whom he left behind with his sister. We understand his financial struggles after he receives a call from his bank warning about the confiscation of his vehicle.

Ashok’s cognitive understanding of self and emotional intelligence add depth to his character.

Costumes of the three lead characters, which are the same throughout the film along with their make-up, also amplify the realism of the film, fitting perfectly into the travel-cinema narrative.

Khanal knew his ways to create a connection between the audience and the screen. With minimal dialogues, the audience, from early on, can get the idea of having to pay close attention to the cinematography, colours, props, and every edge of a frame.

One that stands out the most is the red light inside the truck juxtaposed by the darkness of the outside. Ambience as such gives the film a sense of depth under the warmth, or the discomfort of red.

However, at times, it is almost difficult to put into words the intent of the director. One is compelled to replay some scenes over and over again, simply to understand its underlying motive.

There’s a scene, for instance, where a line of people wearing masks and carrying their belongings walk in a corner of a moving frame. But it is not clear what Khanal is trying to imply with it. After all, why were the people there? Why in a single line? Why were they carrying their belongings and where were they going? Questions like these remain unanswered.

This ambiguity further enters the moral terrain inhabited by the film’s characters. Scenes of dispute and altercation also follow the journey. Yet, every character is given their own motivation and moral ground, resisting the easy division between right and wrong.

Therefore, the film pivots toward a moral question. And Sher Bahadur seems to be the most affected by it. His character, initially a grieving father and a culturally restrictive father-in-law, slowly melts into a man capable of introspection.

‘Chiso Maanchhe’ may seem like it has a slow pace. And it certainly does. But rather than a drawback, it is the film’s conscious choice to demand patience from its viewers.

In the end, the film leaves a corpse, an unrequited love, and a society in transition. It asks us to sit in the cold with its characters. Perhaps the coldness is not only theirs.

articles.title: How Dijup Tuladhar uses AI as part of his everyday toolkit
articles.summary:
Working in US healthcare means I frequently encounter terminology and systems that are unfamiliar in the Nepali context. Previously, understanding a new healthcare concept could require hours or days. Now, I can use AI to break down unfamiliar concepts.

I still verify important information through reliable sources. But AI has shortened the distance.

Building Chordpedia

I founded Chordpedia in 2015 after struggling to find chords for Nepali songs online. The biggest challenge was always execution. AI has changed that equation.

With AI-assisted coding and tools such as ChatGPT, I can move from an idea to a prototype or working feature much faster.

Design and prototyping

Tools such as Figma Make, Lovable and Stitch have changed how I move from an idea to something tangible.

Previously, there was a long process between having an idea and being able to interact with a prototype. Now, I can describe a problem, explore different approaches, generate a prototype, interact with it, identify problems and make changes almost immediately.

However, AI has made the process of designing faster yet hasn't necessarily made deciding what to design easier.

User research and feedback

I use AI to process large amounts of user feedback and identify patterns. It can group similar responses, summarise what users are saying and help him look at competitors from different perspectives.

I look at AI as an assistant. AI can help identify patterns and ask questions, but it cannot always understand the context behind a decision—including users, business priorities, organisational culture and technical limitations.

Everyday life

AI is not limited to my professional life. I also use it for travel planning, learning, comparing options and solving technical problems.

One of my favourite things to do is to use AI to challenge my own thinking.

Instead of asking AI to agree with an idea, I ask it to explain why the idea might be wrong, what I could be missing and what an opposing perspective might look like.

articles.title: Mental wellbeing: When a parent goes abroad for work, children can feel a loss that has no end
articles.summary:
When a parent migrates for work, they leave behind fragments of their presence, which, for a child, are never quite enough to make up a whole person.

As parents’ migration for work becomes more normalised in Nepali society, we might be underestimating its psychological cost, a complex understanding of presence and absence in the children’s minds.

Through FaceTime, voice memos, pictures, and videos, their parent’s embrace is known but never truly felt. As a result, they neither become fully connected nor entirely foreign, leading to a sense of ambiguity in their grief.

Sunika Joshi is a mental health professional specialising in trauma, neurodiversity, child and adolescent mental health, and suicide prevention. She is also the co-founder of Lighthouse Neural, a mental health organisation.

Here, she discusses the psychological impact of parental migration on children, how prolonged separation can shape attachment and relationships, and what families can do to protect children’s emotional well-being.

When one parent goes abroad for work, what happens inside a child’s mind in the first few months before the ‘new normal’ sets in?

The new normal depends on who is the caretaker, living arrangements, and sense of security/ safety where they live. Usually, children gradually adapt to new family dynamics.

Initially, children may experience grief-like responses such as sadness, confusion, anger, and somatic complaints like headaches, stomach pain, and sleep issues.

Younger children may show stress in the form of bedwetting, anger issues, and crying over minor issues that are not related to the absence. Adolescents may experience increased worry due to uncertainty, loneliness, and fear.

It can be termed as ambiguous loss, which is a profound sense of loss and sadness that is not death-related; the parent is physically absent but psychologically or emotionally present in some way.

But at the same time, adolescents can also feel a sense of pride if they see it as a sacrifice for the family’s financial security and remain hopeful that their lives will improve—economically and socially.

If the child is young, has the family member explained what migration is and how the living arrangement will change? Is anyone helping the child to make sense of the change? Does the child have access to communicate with the parent who migrated? Questions, as such, matter equally.

There could be many underlying vulnerabilities. If the child has the right support, they can feel hopeful about the future, but if the child is exposed to uncertainty due to debt or illegal ways to go abroad, the risk of being cheated and the family being stressed, the child can also sense the stress and show emotional and behavioral symptoms.

How does prolonged physical absence affect a child’s attachment style? Are these kids more anxious, more avoidant, or does it vary?

What happens during the absence of the parent determines the attachment style. They can be anxious and avoidant. Prolonged separation can increase the risk of both.

Anxious attachment means becoming hypervigilant, fearing abandonment, and worrying about parents’ return, safety, and relationship. Experience emotional vulnerability and loneliness. This attachment happens when caregivers are unable to consistently meet or respond to the young child’s emotional and physical needs. Later in life, they might struggle with anxiety in relationships, making them ‘clingy’ or jealous.

Avoidant attachment means to learn to suppress and avoid emotional conversations, spending time with family, or communicating their issues. Children may become self-reliant and push people away; don’t actively seek out their caregiver for comfort or emotional support. It results when a young child loses a sense of security in their environment. It can lead to suspicion, hostility, and lack of commitment in later relationships.

But these depend on the child’s temperament, the consistency of the substitute caregiver and how communication with the absent parent is handled.

But when caregiving is inconsistent, children are likely to show anxiety, depressive symptoms, and challenges in forming an emotional bond with friends and family.

Can a strong emotional bond survive almost entirely through video calls and voice notes? What gets lost that even daily calls can't replace?

No, physical presence is different than talking on a call. You see the nuances. It is like reading a summary of the book without reading the entire book.

Video calls and voice notes help maintain a sense of connection and can reduce separation anxiety compared to no contact, but cannot fully replace physical presence, especially for younger children.

The child is deprived of physical affection, which is crucial for co-regulation, feeling safe and secure, and forming an attachment to the parent. The child and parent also miss out on the minor, firsthand details of daily routines and what each other's days look like.

Non-verbal communication is largely missing, creating a gap in understanding underlying emotions and in developing attachment through non-verbal cues. And if certain things are not communicated through words or messages, they will be missed.

In the Nepali context, emotional bonds are formed by providing material support in the form of favourite food and gifts. Families do not communicate through words and talk about emotions. In Nepal, fathers, in particular, do not share vulnerability or emotions.

So, this can create a huge gap in building a strong emotional bond as a family. Families would only know about each other through events shared across the device. What gets lost is the bond, trust, and reliability you create through physical presence, making memories by being in the same space and engaging in activities like cooking and celebrating festivals together. Also, passing down the culture, values, knowledge, and the roots of the family/ethnicity/indigeneity.

Is there any age range where a parent’s absence particularly leaves lasting damage?

Yes, in young age and in adolescence.

Younger children, when they have not made sense of the separation and do not understand the change, can show withdrawal and aggression. Early childhood is the time when they learn and understand attachment, love, care, affection, and emotion regulation from their parents, and disruptions in this process can have emotional consequences. Adolescents also face an increasing risk of confusion, loneliness, worry, and uncertainty.

As humans, we are all resilient and can adjust to change, but how a child makes sense of a parent's absence largely depends on the caretaker and guardian, as well as the family's response, the community the child lives in, and the environment.

The connection with the parent can become superficial and may lead to issues with socio-emotional adjustment. A sense of security and trust can also change as the child grows. Psychological well-being declines if more socio-economic challenges arise after migration.

What’s one piece of practical advice you’d give the parent staying behind to protect a child’s emotional development?

Choose a safe and secure place to live and a caregiver. Assess the risk of abuse, assault, discrimination, and neglect from the people around.

Do not pressure the child to take responsibility for the missing parent.

Make sure they understand why the parent migrated; do not expose them to the news of death, accidents, injury, parent separation.

Create space for the child to express their feelings, be vulnerable and if they are showing emotional distress, understand that it can be a reaction to worry and distress.

Do not shut the children and ask them to understand everything.

Help the child to foster a bond with the migrant parent- help them maintain a healthy relationship and communicate.

Avoid putting the child in the middle of adult conflicts about money or return plans.

Seek help from schools, communicate about the change in a child's life.

How does a child’s sense of self develop when one parent exists through a device or a photo rather than a physical presence?

A risk of getting detached from their culture and community surrounds them.

If they are living with relatives, they do not feel a sense of belonging to a family or community. The child will also find it difficult to navigate their emotions toward the parents; they may appreciate the sacrifice and see them as a hero or savior, or they may see them as not being part of the family's struggles and challenges in person.

There might be too much pressure on them to study well, to live with whatever is provided, and not ask for more.

Children also feel pressure to appreciate and repay the sacrifices their parents have made for their future by being overly pressured to excel academically, be smart, and be very ambitious.

This might not provide the child with an area to explore their authentic self, experiment with hobbies and strengths, and make room for any mistake or failure. So living in constant fear and worry and living up to the family’s expectations.

A sense of safety can be hampered.

If the children are taking the role of caretaker and replacing the parent who migrated, girls tend to start taking care of siblings, cooking and cleaning- all household chores. Sons might feel the responsibility for the family’s safety and security. There may be a mutual understanding of sharing struggles and burdens.

Is there a psychological difference between a parent who is dead, divorced, or absent due to migration?

Yes, migration is a different kind of grief. It is an ambiguous loss. The parent is alive and connected through video calls or messages but not present physically. It comes with uncertainty about when they will return, whether they are ever coming back, and also fear of separation from parents, breaking the family apart, and the uncertainty can prolong distress.

Children can also live in emotional conflict- they can feel guilty for being angry at the parent who sacrificed for the family and confused about what to feel.

Death is an irreversible loss and also a socially recognised loss followed by rituals according to the religion they follow. Grieving is mostly getting to terms with the fact that it is permanent and making sense of the loss- physically and emotionally.

Divorce is often breaking off the family dynamics; even if parents are present physically, it also comes with arrangements of who the child lives with and coming to terms with living separately, but both parents are alive.

Do these children struggle more with trust and intimacy later in life, in friendships or romantic relationships?

Trust and intimacy in later life—yes, it can create difficulty in forming strong relationships, trust and feeling secure.

Lower emotional closeness and less contact with parents and family. Causes difficulty trusting others and forming intimate relationships in adulthood. It can also show up in the form of fear of abandonment, getting into unhealthy relationships, and risk of addiction, and not understanding how relationships should be.

Either giving too much or giving too little. Can get into abusive relationships and not be able to recognise it or get out of it. Not understanding the emotional needs of a partner, as well as feeling like not being understood.

articles.title: Exhibit review: When an oral story becomes a painting
articles.summary:
Artist Bivas Rai’s solo exhibition ‘Myth & Memory’ will open at Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, on August 28.

Presented by the Australian Himalayan Foundation (AHF) and Siddhartha Art Gallery, the exhibition brings together paintings that explore Kirati Rai culture through Sakela, a communal dance and festival celebrated to honour nature and ancestors.

Rai, recipient of the 2025 AHF Himalayan Art Award, grew up in an extended Rai family surrounded by stories. As a child, however, he says he rarely had the patience to listen to them. Years later, his relationship with those stories has changed.

“Indigenous history is primarily passed down in the form of stories from one generation to the next,” says Rai. His growing curiosity about the stories he once avoided led him to spend the past year observing, listening to, and archiving accounts shared by elders in his family.

Rather than trying to establish a single authoritative version, ‘Myth & Memory’ works within this shifting nature of folklore.

Sakela provides the visual language for the series. Its silli, or dance movements, often imitate elements of nature, including animals and flowers. While Sakela sets the visual tone, Rai says the exhibition is rooted in sisterhood and matriarchy.

Every painting in the series features one of his sisters. Rai connects the women he grew up with to the Kirati myth of Tayama and Khiyama, the primordial sisters, allowing familial memory and inherited mythology to occupy the same space.

“My world has been shaped entirely by the strength and presence of my mother, her sisters, and my own sisters,” says Rai.

Through ‘Myth & Memory’, these recollections are carried from oral storytelling into painting, preserving them while acknowledging that memory itself continues to shift each time a story is retold.

The exhibition will be inaugurated by Australian Ambassador to Nepal Simon Ernst, AHF Chair Garry Weare, and AHF Himalayan Art Award founder Margie Thomas.

Myth & Memory

When: August 28 to September 20Where: Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, KathmanduOpening: August 28, 5:30 pm

articles.title: Sikkim chief minister unveils ticket, T-shirt for Nepathya concert
articles.summary:
Nepal’s folk-rock band Nepathya’s upcoming concert in Sikkim has received official backing from the state government, with Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang –Golay, unveiling the event’s ticket and specially designed T-shirt.

Tamang launched the two items during a ceremony in Gangtok on Saturday marking India’s 80th Republic Day. Nepathya had earlier announced that it would perform at Paljor Stadium in the Sikkim capital on October 31.

The concert will be the band’s fourth performance in Sikkim and its biggest there to date, according to the organisers. Nepathya’s first concert in the state was held indoors after the band’s return to the music scene. Its subsequent outdoor performances took place in Pakyong, on the grounds opposite St Xavier’s School, and Rabangla, on the shore of Cho Jo Lake.

Organised by Positive Vibes Entertainment Network, the Gangtok concert aims to promote Sikkim’s music and culture, encourage young people’s creativity and showcase the state’s natural beauty, the organisers said.

Tenzing Dorje, coordinator of the organising team, thanked Tamang for publicly supporting the event.

“We are eagerly looking forward to welcoming Nepathya, one of Nepal’s leading musical groups, to Sikkim,” Dorje said.

Nepathya lead singer Amrit Gurung said the band had consistently received a warm reception in Sikkim and Darjeeling, where several generations have grown up listening to its songs on local radio stations.

“We have been receiving encouraging news about the concert for quite some time, which has further boosted our enthusiasm,” Gurung said.

Nepathya will also perform in Itahari on November 4 and is preparing for a concert in Kirtipur. The band is scheduled to tour South Korea this year and is planning performances in several Nepali cities and abroad towards the end of the year.

Gurung will be joined in Gangtok by Dhruv Lama on drums, Subin Shakya on bass guitar, Niraj Gurung on guitar, Shanti Rayamajhi on madal and Dineshraj Regmi on keyboards.

Tickets for the Gangtok concert can be purchased online through Nepathya’s official website.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Hamilton
articles.summary:
Hillcrest functions as the primary campus neighbourhood for Hamilton, operating essentially as the city's main student hub. Rather than a quiet suburban zone, Hillcrest is highly energetic and packed with student flats, local takeaways, and young people walking to lectures. The neighbourhood is completely dominated by university culture, making it the central gathering point for the local international student community.

People can save time and money because they can walk to classes and the university library within minutes, completely eliminating daily bus or parking costs.

Housing demand is incredibly high at the start of semesters, meaning competition for good rooms is fierce, and properties can suffer from student-related noise.

Silverdale serves as a peaceful alternative to the busier streets of Hamilton. It functions as a relaxed retreat where students can study quietly but still reach campus in under five minutes.

Rents are reasonable, and the neighbourhood offers a much calmer, quieter environment that is perfect for focused study.

The area lacks its own major nightlife or dining scene, so people will have to travel to neighbouring suburbs for entertainment or grocery shopping.

Nawton is a well-established residential suburb located on the western side of Hamilton, far from the main university campus. It serves as an excellent hideaway for budget-conscious students who want to escape the university bubble completely.

Weekly rental prices here are among the lowest in the entire city, letting you get a much larger room or property for a lower price.

The commute to the university is long and requires catching a bus through the city centre.

Dinsdale sits elevated on the western hills of Hamilton, acting as a highly independent and fully self-contained suburban community. Rather than just a collection of houses, it features its own comprehensive shopping centres, supermarkets, and medical clinics that cater to all daily needs.

Access to the local amenities means people can buy cheap groceries and essentials right on their doorstep.

Distance from the eastern campus means people are completely dependent on public transport schedules or owning a car to get to their classes.

Hamilton East

Hamilton East is one of the city’s oldest and most character-filled suburbs, blending a trendy heritage vibe with student living. It serves as a creative bridge perfectly positioned right between the university campus and the central business district.

It offers the lifestyle balance in Hamilton, giving students immediate access to food, local employment opportunities, and vibrant weekend river walks.

The charming, older character homes can be poorly insulated, making them quite cold and expensive to heat during the damp winter months.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Hamilton.

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
Two Nepalis were killed after being hit by a train in Romania’s eastern city of Bacău early Sunday morning. Their identities have not yet been disclosed.

According to a statement from the Bacău Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU), the two were struck by a train at around 3:21 am while walking along the railway line near Chimiei Street.

Emergency responders, including ambulances, rescue teams and medical personnel, reached the site shortly after receiving information about the incident. They found both individuals dead upon arrival, the ISU said.

Romanian police and railway authorities have launched an investigation into the accident.

“An investigation is underway to establish how they ended up on the railway line and the circumstances that led to the accident,” the ISU said in its statement.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.

Lawyer Pandey said the tougher environment has affected not only prospective students but also those already in Australia. Renewing student visas, switching back to student visas after completing post-study work arrangements, and bringing spouses as dependants have all become more difficult, he said.

Obtaining permanent residency has also become significantly more challenging compared with previous years.

Despite the tightening measures, Nepal remains one of the largest sources of international students in Australia. Government data shows Nepali students account for around nine percent of Australia's international student population, making Nepal the third-largest source country.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: प्रमका प्रमुख सल्लाहकार कुमार बेन नै छड्के अनुगमनमा
articles.summary:
प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहका प्रमुख सल्लाहकार कुमार बेन नै एक सरकारी कार्यालयमा छड्के गर्न गएको पाइएको छ। त्यस कार्यालयमा बेन पुग्दा ५५ कर्मचारीमध्ये १४ जना अनुपस्थित थिए। अनुपस्थितमध्ये एक जना कार्यालय प्रमुख नै थिए। गत साउन १९ गते बिहान ९ बजेपछि सेवाग्राहीका रूपमा बेन ललितपुरको लगनखेलस्थित मालपोत कार्यालयमा छड्के/अनुगमन गर्न पुगेका थिए। बेनको निवास त्यहाँबाट नजिकै छ।

बेन त्यस कार्यालयमा केहीबेर बसे। उनी त्यहाँ बस्दासम्म कार्यालय प्रमुख छवि नेपालीसहित १४ कर्मचारी कोही आएनन्। अनुगमनका क्रममा उनी कार्यालय प्रमुखको कार्यकक्षसहित विभिन्न कोठामा पुगेका थिए तर धेरैजसो कोठा खाली थिए। उनले कोठा खाली भएको भिडियोसमेत बनाए। १२ सेकेन्डको भिडियो उनले तत्काल भूमि व्यवस्था सहकारी संघीय मामिला तथा सामान्य प्रशासनमन्त्री प्रतिभा रावललाई पठाए। त्यो भिडियोमा सेवाग्राही कार्यालय पुगेको तर कर्मचारी कम भेटिएको प्रस्ट देखिन्छ।

छड्केका क्रममा बेनले आफ्नो परिचय खुलाएनन् र एक छिनपछि त्यहाँबाट हिँडे।

प्रधानमन्त्रीका प्रमुख सल्लाहकार बेन अनुगमनमा आएका बेला आफू कार्यालय जानेक्रममा बाटोमै रहेको कार्यालय प्रमुख नेपालीले बताए। ‘म लगनखेलमा आइसकेको थिएँ। केही बेरमै कार्यालयमा पुगेको थिएँ। म कार्यालयमा समयमै पुग्ने गरेको छु,’ उनले भने।

आफ्नो कार्यालयमा सेवा प्रवाह नियमित रहेको र नरोकिएको दाबी उनले गरे। ‘हामीले सेवा प्रवाहमा कुनै कमी हुन दिएका छैनौं। सेवा प्रवाहलाई अझ प्रभावकारी बनाएका छौं। सेवाग्राहीलाई दुःख दिएका छैनौं।’ प्रधानमन्त्रीका प्रमुख सल्लाहकार बेन अनुगमन गर्न कार्यालय पुगेका दिन १४ कर्मचारी बिदामा रहेको उनले सुनाए।

भूमि व्यवस्था मन्त्रालय स्रोतका अनुसार बेनले भिडियो पठाएपछि मन्त्रालयले तत्कालै उक्त भिडियो राष्ट्रिय सतर्कता केन्द्रमा पठायो र कार्यालयमा अनुपस्थित कर्मचराीलाई कारबाही गर्न अनुरोध गर्यो। मन्त्रालयको अनुरोधपछि सतर्कताले कार्यालयमा अनुपस्थित कर्मचारीलाई स्पष्टीकरण सोधेको छ। आफूसहित अनुपस्थिति भएका कर्मचारीलाई सतर्कताले स्पष्टीकरण सोधेको नेपालीले स्वीकार गरे।

सतर्कता केन्द्रका अनुसार आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा केन्द्रका कर्मचारीले एक हजार ५७७ कार्यालयमा गई अनुगमन, छड्के तथा निगरानी गरेका थिए। त्यसक्रममा नौ हजार ६९७ कर्मचारीले कार्यालय समय पालना गरेको पाइएन।

यसैगरी तोकिएको पोसाक नलगाउने एक हजार ४०४ जना देखिए। सतर्कताले उक्त आवमा ११ हजार १०१ कर्मचारीलाई कारबाही गर्न सम्बन्धित निकायमा लेखिपठाइएको छ। ‘हामीले गरेको छड्के अनुगमनका क्रममा काठमाडौंका दुई/तीन हजार कर्मचारी बिहान ९ बजेदेखि साँझ ५ बजेसम्म कार्यालयमा बसेको वा सेवा दिएको पाइएन,’ ती अधिकारीले भने, ‘बिहानै हाजिरी गर्ने र घर हिँड्ने गरेको देखियो। केही त बिहान आएपछि एकैपटक साँझ ५ बजे पुगी हाजिरी गर्ने गरेको पाइयो।’

मन्त्रिपरिषद् तथा प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालयको निर्देशनअनुसार केन्द्रले विभिन्न टोली परिचालन गरी दिनहुँ छड्के अनुगमन गरिरहेको छ।

articles.title: पाकिस्तानलाई ५-३ ले हराउँदै भारत विश्वकपको दोस्रो चरणमा
articles.summary:
भारतले पाकिस्तानलाई ५-३ गोलले पराजित गर्दै एफआईएच पुरुष हक्की विश्वकप २०२६ को दोस्रो चरणमा स्थान पक्का गरेको छ। रोमाञ्चक र उच्च स्कोर भएको खेलमा भारतले सुरुदेखि नै आक्रामक खेल देखाउँदै पाकिस्तानमाथि दबाब कायम राख्यो।

भारतका लागि कप्तान हरमनप्रीत सिंह र अभिषेकले समान दुई गोल गरे भने हार्दिक सिंहले एक गोल थपे। पाकिस्तानका हन्नान शाहिदले दुई तथा सुफियान खानले एक गोल गरे पनि टोलीलाई हारबाट जोगाउन सकेनन्। पराजयसँगै पाकिस्तान विश्वकपबाट बाहिरिएको छ।

भारतले पाँचौँ मिनेटमै अग्रता लिएको थियो। पहिलो पेनाल्टी कर्नर पाएको भारतका कप्तान हरमनप्रीतले उत्कृष्ट ड्र्याग फ्लिकमार्फत बललाई गोलमा परिणत गरे। त्यसको केही मिनेटमै अभिषेकले उत्कृष्ट व्यक्तिगत कौशल देखाउँदै गोल गरेपछि भारत २-० ले अघि बढ्यो।

२१औँ मिनेटमा हरमनप्रीतले व्यक्तिगत दोस्रो गोल गर्दै भारतको अग्रता ३-० बनाए। त्यसपछि पाकिस्तानले खेलमा फर्कने प्रयास गर्‍यो। हन्नान शाहिदले उत्कृष्ट ड्रिब्लिङपछि गोल गर्दै अन्तर घटाए। २४औँ मिनेटमा अभिषेकले व्यक्तिगत दोस्रो गोल गरेपछि भारत ४-१ ले अघि बढ्यो। त्यसको केही समयमै सुफियान खानले पेनाल्टी कर्नरबाट गोल गर्दै पाकिस्तानलाई पुनः खेलमा फर्काउने आशा जगाए। पहिलो हाफ भारतको पक्षमा ४–२ गोलमा सकियो।

दोस्रो हाफको सुरुआतमै भारतले अर्को गोल थप्यो। पाकिस्तानका खेलाडीले गरेको खतरनाक ट्याकलपछि भारतले पेनाल्टी स्ट्रोक पायो र हार्दिक सिंहले कुनै गल्ती नगरी गोल गरे। ५-२ को अग्रतापछि भारतले बलमा आफ्नो नियन्त्रण अझ बलियो बनायो।

तर अन्तिम क्वार्टरमा पाकिस्तानले आक्रामकता बढायो। हन्नान शाहिदले फेरि गोल गर्दै अन्तर ५-३ मा झारे। त्यसपछि पाकिस्तानले लगातार दबाब सिर्जना गर्दै बराबरीको प्रयास गरे पनि भारतले आफ्नो रक्षापंक्ति सम्हाल्दै खेल जित्यो। पाकिस्तानका लागि भने भारतविरुद्धको हार विश्वकप यात्राको अन्त्य बनेको छ। भारतले भने चिरप्रतिद्वन्द्वीमाथिको शानदार जितसँगै विश्वकपको उपाधि यात्रालाई थप बलियो बनाएको छ।

articles.title: विभिन्न तीन प्रदेशका केही स्थानमा भारी वर्षाको सम्भावना
articles.summary:
हाल देशभर मनसुनी वायुको प्रभाव रहेको छ। हाल मनसुनको न्यूनचापीय रेखा सरदर स्थानको आसपास रहेको छ।

हाल देशभर साधारणतया बादल लागेको छ। कोशी, बागमती, गण्डकी, लुम्बिनी, कर्णाली र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका केही ठाउँमा हल्कादेखि मध्यम वर्षा भइरहेको जल तथा मौसम विभाग, मौसम पूर्वानुमान महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।महाशाखाका अनुसार आज दिउँसो पनि साधारणतया बादल लाग्नेछ। हिमाली भूभागका केही स्थानमा मेघगर्जन र चट्याङसहित मध्यमसम्मको वर्षा र हिमपातको सम्भावना छ।

पहाडी भूभागका धेरै स्थान, बागमती, गण्डकी, लुम्बिनी र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका तराई भूभागका केही स्थान तथा मधेस प्रदेश साथै कोशी प्रदेशको तराई भूभागका थोरै स्थानमा मेघगर्जन-चट्याङसहित मध्यमसम्म वर्षाको सम्भावना छ। कोशी, बागमती, गण्डकी, कर्णाली र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका पहाडी भूभागका एक-दुई स्थानमा भारी वर्षाको सम्भावना छ।

कोशी प्रदेशको तराई र मधेस प्रदेशका केही स्थानमा हुरीबतासको सम्भावना रहेको महाशाखाले जनाएको छ। त्यसैगरी, आज राति देशका हिमाली र पहाडी भूभागमा साधारणतया बादल लाग्नेछ। कोशी र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशको तराईमा साधारणतया बादल तथा बाँकी तराई भूभागमा आंशिक बादल लाग्नेछ। देशका हिमाली भूभागका केही स्थानमा मेघगर्जन र चट्याङसहित मध्यमसम्मको वर्षा र हिमपातको सम्भावना छ।

पहाडी भूभागका केही स्थानमा मेघगर्जन र चट्याङ्गसहित मध्यमसम्म वर्षाको सम्भावना छ। कोशी र लुम्बिनी प्रदेशको तराई भूभागका केही स्थान, मधेस तथा बागमती, गण्डकी र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशको तराईका केही स्थानमा मेघगर्जन र चट्याङसहित मध्यमसम्मको वर्षाको सम्भावना रहेको महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: ममा शासकीय घमण्ड र सत्ताको लोभ छैन : गृहमन्त्री गुरुङ
articles.summary:
गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङले आफूमा शासकीय घमण्ड र सत्ताको लोभ नभएको बताएका छन्।

ललितपुर महानगरपालिकाले बालकुमारीदेखि बल्खुसम्म जडान गरेको ‘स्मार्ट स्ट्रिट लाइट’को शुभारम्भ कार्यक्रममा उनले यस्तो बताएका हुन्। उनले देश र समाजका लागि सकारात्मक काम गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता समेत व्यक्त गरे।

साथै, नागरिकको सेवामा ललितपुर महानगरपालिकाले गरेको काम प्रशंसनीय र उदाहरणीय रहेको पनि गुरुङले बताए। उनले महानगरपालिकाले कला, संस्कृति र सभ्यताको संरक्षणमा गरेको काम अनुकरणीय रहेको बताए।
